I'm afraid it's just as much nonsense as Luton Airport! 

The implication is that the "interference fringes" are somehow being drawn on the monitor/TV set and then a reconstruction light is used to reconstruct the hologram (from where?). The implication is also that this set of "interference fringes" are being refreshed at video rate. 

Firstly, no TV or monitor can possibly resolve even a modest holographic fringe density of 1000 l/mm or structures of about a micron, or about 25,000 dpi. This frequency is what the film records when you make a transmission hologram with 514nm at about 30 degrees. Note: transmission hologram, not the obvious reflection holograms they were showing. Even if they could get a monitor to show 25,000 dpi and they were reconstructing a transmission hologram, there would be severe dispersion - all you'd see is a colour blur! To show a reflection hologram, as they seem to be doing, you'd need approximately 3000 l/mm or 75,000 dpi, and this is for image plane holograms. To show an object in free space several inches away from the screen, you'd need resolutions of several hundred thousand dpi.

Secondly, it's simply not possible today to transmit 100,000 dpi of organised data at 30 frames/sec through space to several TV sets. The "source" or "camera" would have to calculate the FT of an image, transmit the fringes through space, have the "TV" draw out the fringes (or display them simultaneously by an addressible set of pixels) and then do this again 30 milliseconds later!

You don't need "head tracking" to see a hologram. The eye position does not have to be fixed in any relation to the image, since the image field is an optical wavefront. All of you who make holograms I'm sure don't pass around "head tracking" hardware before you show your holograms to your friends!

What this is, probably, is simply an auto-stereoscopic display with head tracking. The left eye and right eye images are focused in space (possibly via a HOE - which is why they're saying it's "holographic" ) and the focused pair of spots is then moved according to head position by the head tracking equipment. This solves two problems:

1. You can have multiple pairs of auto-stereo positions

2. You can watch the auto-stereo signal even if you move your head.

One problem with auto-stereo is that the eye positions are fixed in space. If you move out of the focused, virtual eye positions, you lose the 3D. Your eyes have to be within the virtual apertures. This is one way they've been working on to cause "real time" focused auto-stereo pairs.

But, it ain't "holographic TV".

The essential point of a hologram is that it exudes a wavefront, not a stereo pair directed to different viewpoints. Accomodation and disparity are "tricks" created to fool the eye into seeing 3D, but 3D is interpreted in the brain, not received and interpreted by the eye. The brain has no specific area for 3D, such as Broca's Area or Wernicke's Area for language. The brain interprets "3D" by means of depth cues and stereo systems simulate those cues by taking advantage of disparity, occlusion and and accomodation. This is not new. Ptolemy's "optics", written around 100AD, goes into great depth (sorry!) about disparity and accomodation. Abu Ali Al-Hasan ibn Al-Hazan ibn Al-Haytham (Alhazen) wrote an almost definitive work of 3D vision in his Book of Optics in the 11nt century AD. He was the first to realise that objects were perceived by light emanating from an object, and not the other way around. Alhazen also compared and differentiated stereo vision with the cyclopean eye. Most of this stuff was forotten during the Dark Ages and rediscovered as late as the mid-19th century.

But I digress.

The pseudoscopic image would reconstruct right on top of the orthoscopic, ie the psi and psi* would occur almost on top of each other. To all intents and purposes, such a view would be impossible to see. This was the problem that plagued holography and almost led to its disappearance until the Leith-Upatniks geometry. There are many papers throughout the 50's on how to solve the "Gabor Problem", particularly by El Sum et al. Also, would the camera see 3D? Is there any advantage to such a system in terms of the characteristics of a hologram?

> **PinkysBrain:** since light doesn't go around corners

Isn't that exactly what diffraction is? See, for instance, the great debates between Newton and Grimaldi/Fresnel/Fraunhofer

From the Seereal site:

*"...Holography you don’t have this limitation because you use the same information as you see in real life.”*

Neither do you with a lenticular

*“One of the most dramatic changes H3D brings about is the functionality, which allows several users watching the same set to focus on different scene points – concurrently! ..."*

Not so, depends on the size of the H1. If you shoot a 4x5 H2 using a 4x5 H1 and I doubt even one person could see it without some effort. A single beam Denisyuk can be seen by a multitude of viewers, dependant on the angle subtended at the plate by the image. However, again, usually not more than about 3 or 4 simultaneously.

*“With the viewer having total control over what they actually focus on is one thing but the subtlety of H3D is that when each viewer picks their point of focus in the scene, the rest of the scene naturally blurs much the same as it does in the real world..."*

Again, not so. This is not an autostereoscopic system - such as I believe the authors think of it - but a wavefront reconstruction system. There is no one position where the eye views come into focus. In the real world, the "scene" does not blur out as if the real world were an autostereoscopic system. If that were so, it'd be impossible to drive. At least, don't drive anywhere near me! Joking!

*"...Parallax can always be adjusted with H3D display as long as the original scale proportions are maintained. Remembering also that parallax is the strongest depth cue, you can see that convergence still has a major role to play in capturing usable images..."*

Parallax in a holographic system is inherent in the system by virtue of the phase relations in the reconstructed wavefunction. The exponential factor in the wavefunction codes for parallax and is coded by the scene being recorded. The "original scale proportions" (whatever they are) has nothing to do with it. The "scaling" of a hologram, by reconstructing with a different lambda as in the original Gabor paper, carries the exponential function with it. The lateral magnification of a hologram recorded at, say, lambda_1 and recosntructed at, say, lambda_2, is given by:

M(lat3) = {1 + z(0)(1/(mu*z(p) - 1/z(r)}(^(-1)

where mu = lambda_1/lambda_2

z(0) = z coord of object point

z(r) = z coord of recon point

lat3 = lateral magnification of the 3rd term (the so-called orthoscopic image)

For the other image:

M(lat4) = {1 - z(0)(1/(mu*z(p) - 1/z(r)}(^(-1)

lat(4) = lateral magnification of the fourth term

By the way, these 3rd and 4th terms refer to the holographic expansion after reconstruction. So, if you constructed a hologram with a reference beam r and an object beam o(x,y), and then reconstructed it with the original reconstruction beam r, then the intensity of the transmitted beam is given by the transmissivity of the recorded plate, t(x,y) and the "output" beam is:

u(x,y) = r*t(x,y) =a*|t|r + b*t*|r| + c*o(x,y) + d*o*(x,y)

Note the third term (c*o(x,y) ) is the original object beam and the 4th term( d*o*(x,y) is the conjugate of the object beam. The first two terms simply add an overall increase in the photosensitive reaction; what I call the "dc" level

There are other points in the Seereal publication, but the whole tenet of the document is that they seem to think that holography is some sort of autosterescopic system based on cues such as disparity, accommodation and occlusion. There are also other 3D cues, such as motion parallax, colour saturation, apparent height etc etc. However, they seem to be missing the fact that this is a method of wavefront reconstruction by diffractive processes. In a diffractive process, the entire wavefront is present to both eyes simultaneously, not to each eye individually.

By the way, all their arguments about the wonders of holography are true (to a greater extent) by lenticulars

> **PinkysBrain:** the holographic image corresponding to a zone plate is a point ..

There is no zone plate. The "zone plate" is a mathematical model used in the early, pre-Kogelnik, days. The hologram was modeled as a series of Fresnel zone plates of varying spacing. Also, there is no point. The focused images from both lens and hologram would be a point spread function: ideally an Airy disc from the lens; the point spread function from the hologram would depend on the bandwidth. 

Remember that the radius of a zone plate is:

r = sqr rt(n*f*lambda)

So, assuming that you have a bandwidth of d(lambda), the range of radii in the zone plate would be:

dr = 1/2{lambda*n/f)^(-1/2)df + (f*n/lambda))^(1/2)d(lambda)}

So, you see there'd be multiple focii. The original model assumed a zero bandwidth because the original models did not take swelling and other factors into account. The "ideal" hologram had no bandwidth. The later models used an MTF concept, which was quite successful until Kogelnik. However, again, the MTF model assumed a zero bandwidth. The laser used for recording these mathematical holograms had an almost infinite coherence length (mathematically, that is). There is still an impression that all lasers emit at a single frequency (eg "633" for HeNe's) which would imply an infinite coherence length. The MTF model did describe the consequences of scattering within the emulsion, which Kogelnik does not address.

However, here we have only two focii, that of the lens and that due to a set of convex fringes within the emulsion. There are no zone plates. Besides which, the zone plates model was used to model Raman Nath diffraction in thin holograms and my hologram would not be thin; I can always coat the lens such that Q > 10. 

Of course, you see the extrapolation; what if the transparency were replaced by an lcd having it's own set of fringe, ie the image on the lcd is a set of fringes. Then you'd have two sets of focused fringes. Each set of focused fringes would then also be a hologram. You have now possibly four holograms: two from the pattern on the lcd, one from the focused lens and one from the convex fringes on the emulsion on the lens. It gets even more interesting since the fringes on the lcd are necessarily Raman Nath, thus each set of fringes from the lcd would have multiple orders. You now have a sinc function superimposed on a diffracted field function from the lens on top of a Kogelnik coupled wave function. In other words, an unholy mess!

posts.content_md:
> **PinkysBrain:** how exactly would you suggest recording a HOE functioning as an on axis lens?

Several methods:

1. Coat a plane piece of glass with dcg. Shoot a hologram on this pane glass, one beam normal and collimated, the other diverging from some point from the other side. Let's say the other beam, the diverging one, diverges from a point f_2 away from the plate. Now, when one side is hit with a colimated beam, the diffracted beam will focus at a point f_2 - a simple lens. Lift the emulsion and place it on the surface of a lens. Yes, this can be done, we've already done it. Of course, there will be some distortion going from a flat surface to a curved surface, but you can always choose a ratio of areas to minimise this. Now you have a glass lens that focuses at f_1 and a holographic lens that focuses at f_2. Actually the focus will be slightly different than f_2 because of distortions, but the difference (delta(f_2) can be made arbitrarily small.

2. Coat one surface of a lens with dcg; tricky because of coating on a curved surface but possible, again we've done this. Now hit the coated side with a planar beam and the other side with a diverging beam from any point other than f_1, but closer to the lens than f_1. This diverging light hits the light and diverges even more because it point of origin is within the focal length of the glass lens. Thus there appears to be a virtual source for the diverging beam coming the other side of the lens, the uncoated side. As far as the dcg is concerned, there's one beam - a planar beam - from one side of the plate and a diverging beam apparently originating from some point - albeit virtual - from the other side at a point which we'll call f_2. When this hologram is developed and the coated side is hit with a collimated beam, the glass lens focuses at f_1 and the fringes in the dcg cause a focus at f_2.

Putting some numbers in. Let's say that the glass lens has a focal length of 10cm. Then a collimated beam from one side will focus at 10 cm from the lens on the other side. Now coat one side with dcg. To record,you hit the coated side with a collimated beam and let's say that you place a point source at 3 cm from the other side (the uncoated side). Then a point source will appear to come from a point 4.3 cm from that side (still the uncoated side). Thus the two beams will create a HOE on the coated side of the lens with a focal length of 4.3 cm. Now, a collimated beam from the coated side will create a focused spot at 10cm away at the other side of the lens (due to the zero order being refracted by the lens) and another spot 4cm away at the other side of the lens (due to the diffraction from the dcg HOE).

We have recently been made aware of this discussion. Thank you for spending so much of your time for discussion of our technology. If you are interested we would be glad to clarify a few principle questions.

A wavefront is not a Fourier Transform. A Fourier transform is a mathematical operation that represents any function, in particular a wave function, into an infinite series. A real 3D scene does not generate a Fourier Transform, it generates a wavefunction in which is embedded a phase relationship. It's the act of sending the phase information to two eyes and the brain calculating the phase difference between the paths to the two eyes that "generates" 3D. Thus:

> **hologuru:** each eye pupil through which the holographic 3D scene is visible.
 

each eye cannot alone see 3D. In holography, every (sinusoidal) Fourier component of the reconstruction wave is diffracted through (a) specific angle(s) by every (sinusoidal) component of the diffracting structure - the fringes. Thus the hologram is mathematically a convolution/correlation integral over the reconstruction wavefunction and the diffracting structure function. Sending the same wavefuntion to both eyes simultaneously is superfluous, or, at best, narrows the viewing aperture and creates 2 2D scenes from a 3D scene. The MIT system, which is apparently what's at work here, does roughly the same, but the scene is not focused at the eye, it 'focuses' or 'coagulates' in mid space. You actually demonstrated that you did! There are basically two forms of diffraction - Raman nath and Bragg. In Bragg, the diffracting structure can be seen as a set of partially reflecting mirrors inside the medium. These mirrors are ideally all at a fixed distance apart and 'pointed' in the same direction (not so for a real display hologram, the 'mirrors' are separated by several distances and pointed in several directions). Anyway, these mirrors are effectively a directional AR coating, or dichroic filter, for a specific wavelength. When light of several wavelengths going in several directions impinge on such a structure, then only a specific wavelength in a specific direction is "chosen" to be altered; the rest being destroyed or passing through unaffected.

In Raman Nath diffraction every wavelength component at any angle is diffracted, but in different directions. This kind of structure obeys the grating equation exactly. So, say you have light that's orange, that is, has a wavelength range from 550 to 600nm. Each component of wavelength lambda is diffracted through an angle given by

Not true. The nth order diffraction angle in a thin hologram is given by:

n*(lambda) = d*sin(theta). For the first order, n=1.

There is no "grating period" and no "sub-pixels". These are misunderstandings or metaphors for connection to electronic displays. In an electronic display system, the display is (generally) made up of an array of equal elements, each of which are independently addressable and self luminous. In the modern day, these element are made of sub-elements, each of which is also independently addressable and self-luminous - "pixels" and "sub-pixels". By their very nature and function, these "pixels" and "sub-pixels" change their luminosity and their "colour" by means electronic data submission, upon which is encoded values pertaining to a specific gamma. This is not always, in fact not even usually, true due to negative coefficients in the gamma. I've written a piece on colour perception and the colour chart and it's probably somewhere in that great miasma called the internet. At any rate, the coded electronic data structure is presented to each group of elements - the "pixels" and "sub-pixels" - in order to decode the data and present an image. The relevant characteristics are:

1. the pixels change their value according to a coding scheme (loosly) based on a colour system which assigns luminositioes to colour. Hence the value expression may be denoted by:

V = alpha*(sub_pixel1) + (beta)* (sub-pixel2) + gamma*(subpixel3)

2. the pixels are all of the same size, hence the term "resolution as it appertains to an electronic display

3. the system is raster scanned, each scan varying allowing pictorial data to be presented to the viewer.

In a computer generated hologram, there are basically three methods:

Calculate the entire object wavefunction

Calculate the entire wavefunction but leave out the "dc" term. That is, leave out the I_1 + I_2 term, since this does not contribute to the phase data.

Calculate bits of the object wavefunction.

This last approach is the basis of the binary detour phase method. Note *Binary*, there are only two values, no variations are permitted. The method essentially uses the Shannon-Hartley theorem as well as the sampling theorem of Fourier Transforms to sample the object wavefunction with a series of displaced Dirac Delta functions; the displacement being given by the Shannon Hartley Theorem. Then the plate is divided into a series of cells. Without going into too much detail (at this point, I can if anyone is interested), the size of the cell is given by the intensity of the object waveform at any given point of the plate upon which the cell is centered:

ab = |o(x,y|^2

The cell is dark (completely opaque) except for a "window", whose position is displaced by the phase of the object wavefunction at any given point and whose size depends on the phase factor in the object exponential.. The displacement of the window at any given point causes a displacement of the optical path that exactly corresponds to a recovery of the phase of the object wavefunction at that point. Once all the cells are "written", then the entire hologram is illuminated by a reconstruction beam to reconstruct the hologram

Note, 

the cells are not the same size but depend on the intensity of the object wave

the displaced windows are not in the same position, but depend on the phase of the wavefront

The cells and windows do not change their value depending on an electronic or optical signal. Once "written", they are "set in stone" as it were.

The cells are not individually addressable; the entire system of cells is illuminated *in toto*. There needs to be an external reconstruction wave, without which the hologram is dark.

Lee's method simply has more than one window, nine I think to improve image integrity. Burchardt showed that three windows were better than 9 and still maintained the same image integrity

posts.content_md:
The grating equation for two off-axis input beams is:

m*(lambda) = d*(sin(phi) +/- sin(theta))

where d is the slit width (the 'pixel' size if you will, although 'pixel ' may be vague in this context since electronic digital displays do not obey the grating equation), m is the order and phi and theta are the two beams impinging on the grating. These days the 'm' is never used because holography rarely goes past the first minimum. Back in the 60's the holograms were very, very thin and so you generally went past several of the sinc minima. The +/- is dependent on whether the two beams are on the same side of the plate normal or not (use '+' if they're not). If one of the beams is on-axis to the plate normal, then one of the angles is zero (let's say phi). In this case, the grating equation reduces to the familiar:

m*(lambda) = d*sin(theta)

In which case, the diffraction angle is:

theta = arcsin(m*lambda/d)

If both beams are off-axis, then, assuming you're interested in the theta deviation:

theta = arcsin{m*(lambda) -/+ d*sin(phi)}/d

There's an extra term due to the off-axis geometry.

In either case, the relationship between d ('pixel' size) and wavelength in the most general case is the diffraction angle(s):

lambda/d = sin(theta) +/- sin(phi)

Ok, I went to their site and read this (Holographic 3-D Displays - Electro-holography within the Grasp of Commercialization (SCIYO.COM) ) paper. There are a number of standard misconceptions. They say, for example, that every "pixel" of a hologram contains the entire image. That's not generally true. If you break a single beam Denisyuk into tiny pieces (eg 1mm diameter shards) and then illuminate one of the shards, you won't see the entire image. This idea is a hangover from the days of laser transmission holograms where the object was a long way from the hologram plane. When the object is very near the plate, no small piece can show the entire object. They also say that the hologram has a "large diffraction angle", then give the space-bandwidth product as a measure of the object beam divergence (from Nyquist) , not the diffraction angle. Now, of course, a large object will give a large object beam divergence and so the extremes of the object field will have large diffraction angles. However, I do get the feeling that they're confusing the diffraction angle (ie the angle of the reference to the plate) with the beam divergence of the object (the angle subtended by the object at the plate). There are a number of other instances, but these caught my eye straightaway.

Now, the problem they're addressing is: If the 'hologram has a large diffraction angle' (not clear what that means), then you need a high spatial frequency (true). However, conventional electronic systems don't have the necessary resolution (true, up to a point. A continuous set of fringes is not quantised and so the concept of "pixel" may not be valid). Their solution is to limit the viewing zone of the hologram by computing the eye position and then to create a hologram fringe structure with a low enough spatial frequency over a narrow section of the display (small holographic aperture) such that the diffracted image field also has a narrow aperture and is directed pretty much to the eye (almost a Gabor geometry with a very small film). As the eye moves, the eye is tracked and, at the new eye position, a new hologram is computed and generated over a small aperture with a narrow viewing aperture. These, constantly created, low aperture holograms are referred to as "sub-holograms, except that these sub-holograms don't exist simultaneously but are created in situ - real time, as it were ("apreture" here meaning the aperture over which the fringe structure is created - not the viewing aperture). The idea is that as you move the eye, the part of the hologram that you would have seen, had it been a 'conventional' hologram would be created as a "sub-hologram" subtending only that part of the image at the eye. I'm not sure how they deal with peripheral vision, but we'll let that pass.

It's a clever idea. There are however a number of issues with that. Firstly, this is clearly a transmission geometry. The light source is behind the display. The light source illuminates the display and so reconstructs the(momentary) sub hologram. In this situation, there is going to be considerable dispersion, unless they use a laser source to reconstruct. Even with a laser source, the angle of diffraction is pretty small, which means that will will be a large number of diffractive orders. No hologram is ever 100% in practice. In this case, the hologram is probably a amplitude hologram in transmission, which implies a 30% efficiency at best. This means there will be a zero order beam. Due to the narrow diffraction angles, the zero order beam is probably very close to the viewer. In a Gabor hologram, it went directly into the viewers eye. The narrow angle of diffraction will also superimpose the conjugate image very close to the primary image. In a Gabor they're right on top of each other. In this geometry they won't be right on top, but will superimpose slightly. If they're using an LED to reconstruct, then there will be dispersion of the LED itself (the zero order beam) as well as dispersion the object. Assuming a 1 micron feature size and a 50nm bandwidth led, we have:

delta( lambda) = d*cos(theta)*delta(theta)

with delta lambda being 50nm. theta is small, cos(theta) is large and so delta theta is also large.

There a number of other issues, but I think these are the main ones. My...shall we say, aprehension..is the fact that apparently no one has seen a demo of this. I'm a great believer in the Sagan dictum: "Extraordinary claims require extraordinary proof". This is quite an extraordinary claim!
